study.title: Ezekiel 35 O Judgment against Edom for his enmity against Israel
study.overview: This chapter brings a prophecy against the mount of Seir, that is, against Edom, presented as a persistent enemy of Israel. The LORD declares that he is against Edom because his old hostility has turned into opportunistic violence: when Judah was humbled, Edom rejoiced, supported destruction, and wanted to occupy the inheritance of Israel. The text emphasizes that God sees the pride of words, the violence practiced and the joy before the fall of his people. The divine answer is retributive: desolation, death, and permanent ruin, that Edom may know that the LORD is God.

outline.title: The message against the Mount of Seir
outline.explanation: Ezekiel receives command to prophesy directly against Edom, a personified in the mount of Seir. The judgment announced includes destruction of the cities and transformation of the land into desolation, with the purpose of revealing the identity and authority of the LORD.

outline.title: The ancient enmity and the returning blood
outline.explanation: The motive of judgment is the continual enmity against Israel, intensified in the time of distress. Edom took advantage of the vulnerability of Judah, and therefore the sword, death and desolation will fall upon their land and their journeys until it is no longer inhabited.

outline.title: The pride against the inheritance of God
outline.explanation: Edom thought that the ruin of Judah would allow the two lands to be taken for himself, as if the LORD had been removed. God answers that he has heard the blasphemies, has seen evil exaltation, and will do with Edom what Edom hath desired for Israel: total desolation, that the LORD may be recognized again.

study.context: The notes identify this oracle as directed to Edom, neighbor of Israel to the southeast, represented by Mount Seir. The text fits into the context of the fall of Judah before the Babylonians, when Edom would have rejoiced and sought an advantage over the land of Israel. The notes also link the Edomite hostility to the old rivalry between Esau and Jacob, that is, to a historical enmity that has prolonged in concrete action against the people of God.
study.theology: The chapter teaches God's sovereignty over the nations and their active defense of the covenant people. Edom's sin is not only political rivalry, but pride, violence and blasphemy against God by mocking the ruin of his people and imagining that the covenant had lost validity. The theology of the text is retributive: the evil desired to the neighbor returns upon the agent itself, showing that God judges not only external acts, but intentions, words and perverse joy in the face of the suffering of others. It is also noteworthy that the judgment aims to reveal who the Lord is: the God of Israel does not abdicate his authority or revoke his choice for Israel because of the apparent victory of the enemies.

scholarViews.insight: The prophecy goes to Edom, identified by the mount of Seir, and presents its prosperity as temporary despite the fall of Judah; the chapter shows Edom as an example of the enemies of Israel.
The chapter shows that whoever has God against himself will also have the word of God against himself; the cause of confrontation is the hostility of Edom against the people of God.
The ancient enmity between Esau and Jacob continued in the descendants, and the Edomites took advantage of Israel's affliction to hurt him; therefore the desolation announced is just.

questions: What does the text reveal about the way God treats violence and joy before the fall of the other?
How does Edom's attitude expose the danger of interpreting God's discipline as if he had abandoned his covenant?
How can the church today avoid any form of satisfaction with the humiliation of others, especially of other brothers and sisters in the faith?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to reject every form of pride, revenge and commemoration of the ruin of others. In practice, this means watching the words, not rejoicing with the defeat of anyone and resisting the temptation to take advantage of the weakness of the neighbor. He also reminds us to trust that God sees hidden injustices and will do justice at the right time. When others fall, the Christian response must be compassion, sobriety and intercession, not contempt.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not inform in detail the exact date of the prophecy nor allow us to affirm with certainty what specific historical fulfillment each expression of judgment had. It is also not possible to go beyond what the commentators say about possible subsequent destructions of Edom, as this is not fully explained in the passages provided.
